figures.title: Desired over have
figures.caption: Put the order and the supply in the same unit (1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 mcg), then divide what is ordered by what is on hand. Sanity-check the answer: an unusual amount, such as more than 3 tablets, means recalculate before giving it.

lines.label: Tablets or capsules
lines.example: Ordered 1,000 mg, tablets are 500 mg: 1,000 ÷ 500 = 2 tablets

lines.label: Liquids
lines.example: Ordered 375 mg, have 125 mg per 5 mL: 375 ÷ 125 × 5 = 15 mL

lines.label: Convert first: 1 g = 1,000 mg
lines.example: Ordered 750 mg, vial is 1 g per 10 mL: 750 ÷ 1,000 × 10 = 7.5 mL

figures.title: Weight-based dosing
figures.caption: Convert pounds to kilograms before anything else; skipping it more than doubles the dose. Then check the order against the safe range, and hold and clarify any dose above it with the provider.

lines.label: Safe range, divided into doses
lines.example: 200 mg/kg/day × 10 kg = 2,000 mg a day ÷ 4 doses (every 6 hr) = 500 mg

figures.title: IV medication drips
figures.caption: Find how much drug is in each mL of the bag, then divide the hourly dose by it. For per-minute drips, multiply by 60 for the hour, and make the units match (1 mg = 1,000 mcg) before dividing.

lines.label: Concentration in the bag
lines.numerator: Drug in the bag (units or mg)

figures.title: IV flow rate
figures.caption: Pumps run in mL per hour; gravity tubing is counted in drops per minute, so it needs the tubing's drop factor. Round drops to a whole number.

figures.title: Anticoagulants: labs and reversal
figures.caption: Heparin goes with aPTT and protamine, warfarin with INR and vitamin K. PCC is prothrombin complex concentrate. A platelet fall of half or more on heparin suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): stop all heparin, flushes included.
rows: aPTT, 1.5 to 2.5 times control; platelets for HIT
Platelets, CBC, creatinine; no routine aPTT
PT/INR, goal 2 to 3; takes 3 to 5 days to work
Vitamin K; 4-factor PCC for major bleeding
No routine test; kidney function, CBC

figures.title: INR on warfarin
figures.caption: The international normalized ratio (INR) tracks warfarin; heparin is tracked by aPTT. Check it before each dose, and at any high value look for bleeding: gums, urine, black stools, a sudden headache.

bands.label: Below goal
bands.note: About 1 without warfarin. On warfarin it means clot risk: report so the dose can be adjusted.

bands.label: Goal
bands.note: Therapeutic for atrial fibrillation, DVT and PE; give the dose. Mechanical valves: 2.5 to 3.5.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Bleeding risk. Hold the dose, notify the provider and assess for bleeding.

bands.label: Very high
bands.note: Hold warfarin and notify. Expect vitamin K (phytonadione) as prescribed, especially with bleeding.

figures.title: Digoxin level and pulse check
figures.caption: Count the apical pulse for a full minute before each dose: hold below 60 in adults, 70 in children, 90 to 110 in infants. Low potassium makes toxicity likely even when the level is in range.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: May not control the heart rate or heart failure symptoms.

bands.label: Therapeutic
bands.note: In heart failure the goal is the low end, about 0.5 to 0.9.

bands.label: Toxic
bands.note: Anorexia, nausea, yellow-green halos, bradycardia, dysrhythmias. Hold and notify; digoxin immune Fab.

bands.label: Hold
bands.note: Hold the dose and notify the provider.

bands.label: Give
bands.note: Give the dose if potassium and the digoxin level are also in range.

figures.title: Serum lithium
figures.caption: Lithium travels with sodium. Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, heavy sweating, a low-salt diet, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides all raise the level. Teach 2 to 3 L of fluid a day and steady salt intake.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Below the maintenance range; mood symptoms may return.

bands.label: Therapeutic
bands.note: Maintenance range. Draw the level 12 hours after the last dose.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Used short term for acute mania. Side effects increase; watch for early toxicity.

bands.label: Toxic
bands.note: Early toxicity: vomiting, diarrhea, coarse hand tremor, muscle weakness. Hold the dose and notify.

bands.label: Severe
bands.note: Severe toxicity: ataxia, confusion, slurred speech, seizures, dysrhythmias. Dialysis may be needed.

figures.title: Phenytoin and theophylline levels
figures.caption: Both are kept at 10 to 20 mcg/mL. Phenytoin toxicity shows first in the eyes and gait; theophylline toxicity looks like too much caffeine and can progress to seizures. Hold the dose and notify for a level above 20.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Seizures may break through. Ask about missed doses.

bands.label: Therapeutic
bands.note: Gum overgrowth can occur at any level: brush, floss, see a dentist.

bands.label: Toxic
bands.note: Nystagmus first, then drowsiness and an unsteady gait. Hold the dose and notify.

bands.label: Severe
bands.note: Slurred speech, confusion, lethargy, coma.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: May not control bronchospasm.

bands.label: Therapeutic
bands.note: Quitting smoking, ciprofloxacin and erythromycin raise the level.

bands.label: Toxic
bands.note: Nausea, vomiting, restlessness, tachycardia, then dysrhythmias and seizures. Hold and notify.

figures.title: Peak and trough levels
figures.caption: Draw the trough just before a dose (the lowest level) and the peak 30 minutes after an IV infusion ends (the highest). A high trough warns of kidney and ear toxicity; a low peak means the dose is too small.

series.label: Serum level
series.note: Rises during the 30 to 60 minute infusion, peaks, then falls to its trough just before the next dose.

series.label: Peak must reach
series.note: Drawn 30 minutes after the infusion ends. A peak below this line is too low to clear the infection.

series.label: Trough must fall below
series.note: Drawn just before the dose (gentamicin under 2 mcg/mL). Above this, the drug is building up: hold and notify.

figures.title: When insulin works
figures.caption: Hypoglycemia is most likely at each insulin's peak. Rapid-acting goes in with the meal; glargine has no real peak and is never mixed with another insulin.

series.label: Rapid (lispro, aspart)
series.note: Onset about 15 minutes, peak 1 to 2 hours, lasts 3 to 5 hours. Give it with the meal.

series.label: Short (regular)
series.note: Onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 4 hours, lasts 6 to 8 hours. The only insulin given IV.

series.label: Intermediate (NPH)
series.note: Cloudy. Onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, lasts up to 18 hours. Watch for a mid-afternoon low.

series.label: Long (glargine)
series.note: Onset 1 to 2 hours, no pronounced peak, lasts about 24 hours. Never mix it with another insulin.

figures.title: Mixing regular and NPH insulin
figures.caption: Air in: cloudy, then clear. Insulin out: clear, then cloudy, so NPH never gets into the regular vial and slows it. Glargine and detemir are never mixed with another insulin.

steps.title: Check the order and both vials
steps.detail: Right insulins, doses and dates. Roll the cloudy NPH vial gently between the palms; never shake it. Clean both tops.

steps.title: Inject air into the NPH (cloudy) vial
steps.detail: Air equal to the NPH dose. Withdraw no insulin; remove the needle.

steps.title: Inject air into the regular (clear) vial
steps.detail: Air equal to the regular dose. Leave the needle in and turn the vial upside down.

steps.title: Withdraw the regular (clear) dose first
steps.detail: Clear before cloudy. Clear any air bubbles now, while only regular insulin is in the syringe.

steps.title: Then withdraw the NPH (cloudy) dose
steps.detail: Push no regular insulin into the NPH vial. Draw to the exact combined total; if you overshoot, discard and start again.

steps.title: Verify and give subcutaneously
steps.detail: Check both doses and the total, with a second nurse if policy requires. A mixed dose is never given IV.

figures.title: Opioid overdose: naloxone response
figures.caption: Sedation comes before respiratory depression, so check sedation with every set of vital signs. Airway and breathing come first; naloxone is added to them, and it can wear off before the opioid does.

steps.title: Stop the opioid or PCA
steps.detail: Hard to rouse, slow shallow breaths (often below 10/min), falling SpO2, pinpoint pupils. Stop the infusion; hold further doses.

steps.title: Stimulate the client
steps.detail: Call the client by name and shake the shoulder. A client who drifts off mid-sentence is in danger.

steps.title: Support the airway and breathing
steps.detail: Open the airway, raise the head of the bed, give oxygen, and ventilate with a bag-valve mask if breathing is inadequate. Call for help.

steps.title: Give naloxone per protocol
steps.detail: IV in small repeated doses titrated to breathing, not full alertness; too much at once brings severe pain and withdrawal.

steps.title: Watch for re-sedation
steps.detail: Naloxone lasts 30 to 90 minutes, less than most opioids. Check breathing, sedation and SpO2 often for at least 2 hours.

steps.title: Notify and revise the pain plan
steps.detail: Report and document. Expect a lower opioid dose or new PCA settings before the opioid restarts.

figures.title: Giving a blood transfusion
figures.caption: ABO-incompatible transfusions almost always start with an identification error, so the bedside check is the step that matters most. Severe reactions show early: stay for the first 15 minutes.

steps.title: Check the order, consent and IV access
steps.detail: Signed consent and a patent 18- or 20-gauge catheter in an adult. Pick the unit up only when ready; start it within 30 minutes.

steps.title: Prime the tubing with normal saline only
steps.detail: Y-tubing with a blood filter and 0.9% sodium chloride. Dextrose hemolyzes red cells; the calcium in lactated Ringer's clots them.

steps.title: Verify with a second nurse at the bedside
steps.detail: Two client identifiers, ABO and Rh type, unit number and expiration, matched to the wristband, the unit label and the order.

steps.title: Take baseline vital signs
steps.detail: Temperature, pulse, respirations and BP just before starting, so a reaction shows up as a change.

steps.title: Start slowly and stay 15 minutes
steps.detail: Hemolytic and anaphylactic reactions appear early. Recheck vital signs at 15 minutes, then as policy directs.

steps.title: Finish within 4 hours
steps.detail: Bacteria multiply at room temperature. Nothing but normal saline goes through the blood line; no medications.

figures.title: Transfusion reaction response
figures.caption: Chills, fever, back or flank pain, dyspnea, hives or falling BP during a transfusion: stop it first and ask questions later. Never flush the old line, which pushes more of the blood into the client.

steps.title: Stop the transfusion
steps.detail: At the first sign of a reaction. Disconnect the blood tubing at the catheter hub.

steps.title: Keep the vein open with normal saline
steps.detail: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride on new tubing, so the blood left in the old line is not flushed into the client.

steps.title: Stay, assess and take vital signs
steps.detail: Airway, breathing, BP, pulse, temperature. Treat as ordered: fluids for low BP, an antihistamine for hives.

steps.title: Notify the provider and blood bank
steps.detail: Report the signs, the time the reaction began and how much blood has infused.

steps.title: Return the bag and tubing
steps.detail: Send the unit, tubing and labels to the blood bank with the reaction form, plus blood samples as ordered.

steps.title: Send a urine sample
steps.detail: Urine is tested for free hemoglobin, a sign of hemolysis. Watch the output for kidney injury.

steps.title: Document
steps.detail: The reaction, times, volume infused, actions taken and the client's response.

figures.title: IV site complications
figures.caption: Check the site before every infusion and often during it. Whatever the complication, stop the infusion first; a vesicant leak is the one where the catheter stays in long enough to draw back the drug.
rows: Cool, pale, swollen site; the infusion slows
Stop, remove the catheter, elevate the arm, restart elsewhere
The same, plus burning and blanching; later blisters, necrosis
Stop, aspirate through the catheter, notify; antidote such as phentolamine
Red, warm, tender vein; a red streak or hard cord
Stop, remove, warm compress, restart in the other arm
Redness, drainage or pus at the site; fever
Remove the catheter, culture as ordered, notify

figures.title: Safe medication administration
figures.caption: The rights (client, drug, dose, route, time, documentation) are checked at every step, not once. A scanner or smart-pump alert is a reason to stop and verify, never to override.

steps.title: Verify the order is complete and clear
steps.detail: Drug, dose, route, time. Clarify anything illegible, unusual or written with a do-not-use abbreviation (U, QD, 1.0 mg) before giving it.

steps.title: Check allergies and the data the drug needs
steps.detail: Allergies, plus the pulse, BP, glucose or lab value the drug depends on. Hold and ask when a value is out of range.

steps.title: Compare the label with the order
steps.detail: When taking it out, while preparing it and at the bedside. Question a dose far from the usual one, such as several tablets.

steps.title: Identify the client and scan
steps.detail: Two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, against the wristband, never the room number. Replace a band that will not scan.

steps.title: Double-check high-alert drugs
steps.detail: Insulin, heparin, IV opioids, concentrated potassium, chemotherapy: an independent check by a second nurse and the pump drug library.

steps.title: Give it, then document
steps.detail: Stay until an oral dose is swallowed. Document right after giving it, never before.

figures.title: After a medication error
figures.caption: The client first, then the provider, then the paperwork. The chart holds only objective facts; the incident report is a separate quality document that the chart never mentions.

steps.title: Assess the client first
steps.detail: Vital signs and signs of the drug's effect, such as a low BP after an antihypertensive. The client comes before any paperwork.

steps.title: Notify the provider and charge nurse
steps.detail: Report what was given, how much and when, and the client's condition.

steps.title: Carry out orders and keep monitoring
steps.detail: Labs, an antidote or closer observation as ordered, for as long as the drug can act.

steps.title: Document the facts in the chart
steps.detail: What was given, findings, who was notified and the client's response. No blame, and no mention of the incident report.

steps.title: Complete the incident report
steps.detail: An objective account for risk management: what happened, when, who saw it, who was notified. Never filed in the chart.

steps.title: Report near misses too
steps.detail: An error caught before it reached the client is still reported, so the weak spot in the system gets fixed.

figures.title: Antidotes and reversal agents
figures.caption: Pair the drug with its antidote, then support airway, breathing and circulation while it works. Several antidotes wear off before the drug does, so keep monitoring after the client improves.
rows: Shorter-acting than most opioids: watch for re-sedation
Can provoke seizures in long-term benzodiazepine users
Prothrombin complex concentrate is added for major bleeding
For dysrhythmias, severe hyperkalemia or a very high level
Protects the liver; works best within 8 hours of the overdose
Glucagon; IV calcium for calcium channel blockers
Atropine comes first for symptomatic bradycardia
